content: Allergic rhinitis is a prevalent condition that affects both adults and children. It is characterized by symptoms such as nasal obstruction, excessive nasal discharge (rhinorrhea), sneezing, and nasal itching, all of which can significantly impair quality of life. Nasal irrigation, also referred to as nasal douching, washing, or lavage, involves rinsing the nasal cavity with saline solutions, which can be isotonic or hypertonic. This procedure can be performed using various methods, including low positive pressure from a spray, pump, or squirt bottle, a nebulizer, or gravity-based techniques where saline is introduced into one nostril and allowed to drain out of the other. Saline solutions are readily available over the counter and can be used either as a standalone treatment or in conjunction with other therapies. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of nasal saline irrigation in individuals with allergic rhinitis. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Trials Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, with the last search performed on November 23, 2017. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared nasal saline irrigation, delivered by any method and with varying volumes, tonicity, and alkalinity, against either no nasal saline irrigation or other pharmacological treatments in adults and children with allergic rhinitis. Studies that compared nasal saline irrigation to no saline, where all participants also received pharmacological treatments such as intranasal corticosteroids or oral antihistamines, were also included. The review incorporated 14 studies with a total of 747 participants, including 499 children and 248 adults. None of the studies reported outcomes beyond three months of follow-up. The saline volumes used in the studies ranged from very low to high, and both hypertonic and isotonic solutions were employed. When comparing nasal saline irrigation to no saline treatment, seven studies (112 adults and 332 children) were included. These studies used different scoring systems to measure patient-reported disease severity, and the data were pooled using standardized mean differences (SMD). Nasal saline irrigation appeared to improve patient-reported disease severity compared to no saline at up to four weeks (SMD -1.32, 95% CI -1.84 to -0.81; 407 participants; 6 studies; low-quality evidence) and between four weeks and three months (SMD -1.44, 95% CI -2.39 to -0.48; 167 participants; 5 studies; low-quality evidence). Despite the low quality of evidence, the effect sizes were considered large. Subgroup analyses indicated improvements in both adults and children, but analyses based on saline volume and tonicity were inconclusive due to heterogeneity. Adverse effects, such as nosebleeds (epistaxis) or local discomfort, were not reported in two studies (240 children), and three studies reported no adverse effects in the saline group. One study (48 children) assessed disease-specific health-related quality of life (HRQL) using a modified RCQ-36 scale but found no clear differences between groups (very low-quality evidence). No other secondary outcomes were reported. When nasal saline irrigation was used as an adjunct to pharmacological treatments (intranasal steroids or oral antihistamines), three studies (40 adults and 79 children) compared saline with intranasal steroids versus intranasal steroids alone, and one study (14 adults) compared saline with oral antihistamines versus oral antihistamines alone. It was uncertain whether there was a difference in patient-reported disease severity at up to four weeks (SMD -0.60, 95% CI -1.34 to 0.15; 32 participants; 2 studies; very low-quality evidence) or between four weeks and three months (SMD -0.32, 95% CI -0.85 to 0.21; 58 participants; 2 studies; very low-quality evidence). Adverse effects were not systematically reported, but three studies mentioned them. One study (40 adults) reported no adverse effects in either group, while two studies reported no adverse effects in the saline group. It was uncertain whether saline irrigation improved disease-specific HRQL at four weeks to three months compared to pharmacological treatment alone (SMD -1.26, 95% CI -2.47 to -0.05; 54 participants; 2 studies; very low-quality evidence). No other secondary outcomes were reported. When comparing nasal saline irrigation to intranasal steroids, it was uncertain whether there was a difference in patient-reported disease severity at up to four weeks (MD 1.06, 95% CI -1.65 to 3.77; 14 participants; 1 study) or between four weeks and three months (SMD 1.26, 95% CI -0.92 to 3.43; 97 participants; 3 studies). Similarly, no clear differences were observed in disease-specific HRQL between four weeks and three months (SMD 0.01, 95% CI -0.73 to 0.75; 83 participants; 2 studies). Adverse effects were reported in one study (21 participants), which noted two withdrawals due to adverse effects but did not specify the nature of these effects or the group affected. Three studies reported no adverse effects with saline irrigation, although one study noted that 27% of participants experienced local discomfort with steroid use. No other secondary outcomes were reported. In conclusion, nasal saline irrigation may reduce patient-reported disease severity compared to no saline irrigation at up to three months in both adults and children with allergic rhinitis, with no reported adverse effects. However, the quality of evidence was low or very low, and no data were available for outcomes beyond three months. The included studies were generally small and used a variety of outcome measures with unclear validation. This review did not include direct comparisons of different saline types (e.g., varying volumes or tonicities). Given that saline irrigation is a low-cost, safe, and potentially effective alternative to intranasal steroids and antihistamines, further high-quality research in this area is needed.
